how-to-price-a-change-order.html.text:
← Change order margin calculator

How do I price a construction change order?

Change orders get quoted in the least favourable conditions available: on site, under time pressure, usually from wage and materials in someone's head. The base contract was costed carefully with burden, overhead, and margin; the change often is not — and since added scope consumes exactly the same supervision, insurance, and vehicles as contracted work, every change priced that way quietly dilutes the profit on a job that was priced right.

Open the free change order calculator

From scope to a number you can defend

  1. Load the wage with payroll burden, then multiply by the added hours.
  2. Add materials and any subcontractor cost for the direct cost.
  3. Apply your overhead percentage. Direct cost plus overhead is the walk-away price.
  4. Divide by (1 − target margin) for the price to propose — then enter the price you were going to give and see where it lands.

Worked example

Eight added hours at a $28 wage with 25% burden is $280.00 of loaded labour. With $350.00 of materials the direct cost is $630.00; 10% overhead adds $63.00, putting the walk-away price at $693.00. At a 20% target margin the price to propose is $866.25. The instinctive quote here — eight hours at $28 plus materials, or $574.00 — is $119.00 below the point at which the work merely breaks even. And note the markup trap: adding 20% to $693.00 gives $831.60, which is a 16.7% margin, not the 20% intended.

Common questions

How do I price a construction change order?

Cost the added scope the same way you costed the original contract. Load the wage with payroll burden to get a real hourly cost, multiply by the added hours, add materials and any subcontractor cost for a direct cost, apply your overhead percentage, and that total is the walk-away price — the number below which the change loses money. Then divide the walk-away price by one minus your target margin to get the price to propose. Quoting from wage and materials alone skips burden, overhead, and margin.

What is the difference between the walk-away price and the target price on a change order?

The walk-away price is cost recovery: direct cost plus overhead, with no profit at all. Accepting it means the added work is done for nothing, and anything under it is done at a loss. The target price is the walk-away price grossed up for the margin you intend to earn. Knowing both is what makes a negotiation possible — you can concede toward the floor deliberately, and see exactly how much margin each concession costs, instead of discovering afterwards that you went under it.

Should a change order include overhead and profit?

Yes. Added scope consumes the same supervision, insurance, vehicles, and office time as contracted work, and it usually consumes more scheduling attention per dollar because it is unplanned. Many standard contracts and public-works schedules explicitly allow a stated overhead and profit percentage on change orders for exactly this reason. Omitting them prices the change below the cost of performing it and dilutes the margin on the base contract every time one is signed.

Why is my margin lower than the percentage I marked up?

Because a markup on cost and a margin on price are different arithmetic. Marking a $693.00 cost up by 20 percent gives $831.60, which is a margin of about 16.7 percent, not 20. To earn a 20 percent margin you divide by 0.8, which gives $866.25. On a single change order the difference is small; applied to every change across a year of jobs it is a meaningful share of the profit that was supposed to be there.

This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give the customer to approve before the added work begins — your details, theirs, what the change covers, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Common questions

What is the difference between the walk-away price and the target price?

The walk-away price is your cost floor — loaded labor plus materials, subcontractor cost, and overhead, with zero profit. The target price divides that floor by one minus your target margin, so it already has the margin built in. On the defaults (8 hours at $28/hr, 25% burden, $350 materials, 10% overhead, 20% target margin), the floor is $693.00 and the target price is $866.25 — the gap between them is exactly the profit a 20% margin requires.

Why is loaded labor $280 for 8 hours at $28/hour, not $224?

Because payroll burden is applied to the wage before multiplying by hours: hours × wage × (1 + burden). At the default 25% burden that adds $56 — the employer-side taxes and insurance cost of that labor, not profit. Change-order pricing built on the $224 bare-wage number would be quietly working at a loss on every hour billed.

Why does overhead apply to materials and subcontractor cost, not just labor?

Overhead is a percentage of the whole direct cost — loaded labor plus materials plus subcontractor cost — because the business absorbs its overhead on every dollar that flows through a job, not only the payroll dollars. On the defaults that direct cost is $630.00, and 10% overhead on that full figure is $63.00.

What does “above cost, but below your target margin” mean?

It means the proposed price covers your walk-away floor and leaves some profit, just not as much as your target margin asks for. On the defaults, proposing $750 against the $693 floor leaves $57 of profit — but margin is profit divided by price, not by cost, so $57 / $750 is 7.6%, short of a 20% target by 12.4 points. A price can clear cost by a comfortable-looking dollar amount and still miss the margin you were aiming for.

My contract caps change-order markup. Does that change what I can charge?

Yes, and it is the field most likely to change your answer. Enter the cap and the calculator shows the most the contract permits you to bill — direct cost plus that percentage — next to what is left of it after your own overhead. The two come out of the same allowance, so a 10% cap against 10% overhead means the change order earns exactly nothing: on the defaults the cap and the $693.00 walk-away floor are the same number. Below that, at a 5% cap, the most you may bill is $661.50 and every change order on the contract is a loss. Leave the field at zero for a contract with no cap and nothing changes.

The added work pushes the schedule. Where does that cost go?

Into "days added" and "extended general conditions ($/day)" — the supervision, site trailer, and rented plant the added scope keeps on site. It is treated as a direct cost of the change order, so overhead and margin carry on it like any other, which is the point: general conditions absorbed by the contractor are absorbed because they were never in the change order to begin with. Three days at $450 turns a $630 change order into $1,980 of direct cost and moves the target price from $866.25 to $2,722.50. Leave both at zero for work that fits inside the existing schedule.

Why does the cap warning appear before I enter a proposed price?

Because the cap is a fact about your contract rather than about the price you are considering. If the markup the contract allows is below your overhead rate, every change order under it loses money whatever you propose, and waiting for a proposed price would keep that silent on exactly the page you have not finished filling in. The other messages still wait for a proposed price, because they are comparisons against one.

Why is target margin capped at 99%?

The target price divides the cost floor by (1 − target margin). At 100% that division is by zero; the calculator caps the input at 99% so a mistyped margin produces a very large, clearly wrong price instead of an error or an infinite one.

Where is my data saved?

Only in this browser's local storage, as a draft you can return to, and “Copy share link” encodes your entries into this page's own URL hash so a partner or the customer can open the exact numbers you priced. Anonymous feature counts (that you calculated, copied a summary, or copied a share link) are on by default and can be turned off with the button in the footer; Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable them automatically. Nothing you type is uploaded anywhere — a link only travels if you send it.

vs-a-rough-lump-sum.html.text:
← Change Order Margin Calculator

This calculator vs. a rough lump sum

A round-number change-order price is built from what's visible on the takeoff — labor, materials, the sub — rounded up by a margin that feels safe. Two costs that never show up on a takeoff are exactly what it misses.

What a rough lump sum is

A lump sum is the fastest way to price a change order: look at the added scope, add up the labor hours and material cost you can see, pick a number that feels like a comfortable markup over that, and send it. It works well enough often enough that most contractors keep doing it, because writing a full worksheet for a one-day punch-list item is not worth the time.

The guess is built entirely from costs that appear on a takeoff. Two costs that do not routinely get left out: the extra days the added scope keeps a supervisor, a trailer, or rented equipment on the site after the original schedule would have wrapped, and the ceiling a contract's own markup-cap clause puts on what can actually be billed once the contractor's overhead comes out of that same allowance. A lump sum that never asked about either one has no way to know it is short by exactly what they would have added.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the added labor hours, loaded wage, materials, subcontractor cost, the days the schedule slips and what a day of holding the site open costs, your overhead rate, target margin, and your contract's markup-cap percentage — zero if it has none. It returns a walk-away cost floor, a target price, and, when a cap applies, what the cap actually permits to bill and what margin survives once overhead comes out of it.

A rough lump sumThis calculator
Adds up the labor, materials, and sub cost visible on the takeoff, then rounds up by a margin that feels comfortable. Loads the entered wage by your payroll-burden percentage and adds materials and subcontractor cost the same way, so the starting cost is not a guess.
Has no line for the days the added scope keeps a supervisor, a trailer, or rented equipment on site — extended general conditions get absorbed rather than billed. Prices the days added at your entered daily general-conditions rate as its own direct cost, carried through overhead and margin like any other line.
Does not check the price against a contract's markup-cap clause, so a guess can be billed above what the cap actually allows. Applies the entered markup cap to cost and reports the billable ceiling and the margin left after overhead — before the change order is sent, not after it is disputed.
Gives one number, with no visibility into what happens to margin if the cap and the overhead rate leave less room than the guess assumed. Shows the walk-away floor, the target price, and the capped price side by side, so a cap that quietly erases the margin is visible before work starts.

A worked example, computed from this calculator's own arithmetic: a scope change needs 24 labor hours at $32/hour with 28% burden ($983.04 loaded), $1,800 in materials, and a $2,200 subcontractor, and adds 4 days to the schedule at $350/day in general conditions (supervision, trailer, rented equipment) — $1,400. Direct cost is $6,383.04; with 10% overhead, the walk-away price is $7,021.34, and a 20% target margin would call for a price of $8,776.68. A lump-sum guess built only from the visible labor, materials, and sub cost ($4,983.04) and rounded up to $6,000 to feel safely profitable is actually $1,021.34 under the walk-away floor, because it never priced the four days the job site stayed open. A higher guess of $7,500 clears that floor — but this contract caps change-order markup at cost plus 15%, which permits billing only $7,340.50, nowhere near the $8,776.68 the target margin called for. The extra $159.50 above the cap would be disputed or unbillable, and what survives the cap after overhead is a 4.3% margin, far short of the 20% target the contractor thought they were pricing to.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Why does a rough lump sum under-price a change order?

Because it is built from the costs a contractor can see on the takeoff — labor hours, materials, a subcontractor's number — rounded up by a margin that feels comfortable. Two costs that do not show up on a takeoff routinely get left out entirely: the extra days the added scope keeps a supervisor, a trailer, or rented equipment on site, and the ceiling a contract's own markup cap puts on what can actually be billed once overhead comes out of the same allowance. A guess that never asked about either one is short by exactly the amount they would have added.

Can a change order price above cost still lose money?

Yes, once a contract's markup cap is in the picture. Many change-order clauses cap markup at a percentage of cost — "cost plus 15%", for example — and that allowance has to cover the contractor's own overhead as well as profit. A guess that clears the walk-away cost floor can still land above what the cap actually permits to bill, or clear the cap but leave only a few points of margin once overhead is taken out of it, and a round number gives no way to see which one happened before the work is done.

What does a rough lump sum get right?

For a small, fast change with no schedule impact and a contract with no markup cap, a quick round-number guess set comfortably above the visible labor and material cost can land close enough. The risk is the guess not knowing which change orders that is true for — a lump sum that worked on last week's punch-list item does not know that this week's change adds four days to the schedule or runs into a 15% cap.

Does this calculator know what markup my contract allows?

No. It has no access to your contract. You enter the markup cap percentage from your own change-order clause — zero if there is none — and the calculator applies it to the cost it computed, showing what is actually billable under the cap and what margin that leaves after overhead. Reading the clause is still yours to do; the arithmetic once you have is what this replaces.

← Change Order Margin Calculator

This calculator vs. Buildertrend

Two different shapes: Buildertrend is an account-based platform for running a whole construction project. This page is a free, private, no-account worksheet for one number — whether a single change order's proposed price actually clears your cost floor and target margin.

What each tool is for

Buildertrend is a construction project-management platform founded in 2006 by Dan Houghton and Jeff and Steve Dugger, headquartered in Omaha, Nebraska. It is built around running a job end to end — scheduling, budgets, purchase orders, client communication, daily logs, and change orders, all tied to one project record that a builder, remodeler, or specialty contractor and their client both log into over the life of the job. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across projects, not a one-off calculator. Buildertrend's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not schedule a job, track a budget across trades, or manage a client portal. It takes one change order's added labor hours, loaded wage, materials, subcontractor cost, schedule delay, overhead, target margin, and contract markup cap, and turns that into a walk-away cost floor, a target price, and — if you have one — a check of whether your proposed price clears both, plus a plain-text approval summary. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
